items.title: Five companies are the entire S&P capex story — and tech is 40% of weight but only 30% of EPS
items.idea: Comm services, cons disc and IT account for functionally all S&P capex since 2024, and inside them it's GOOGL+META, MSFT+ORCL and AMZN. Tech is ~40% of index weight but 30% of EPS, and revenue of more than half the sectors exceeds tech's. Nominal GDP at 6.3% is top-line growth, not profit — the profits are being recycled into capex. MSFT, ORCL and AMZN trade sideways vs the index as capex rises.
items.angle: The capex bid is a handful of balance sheets. If any one of them blinks, the 'AI investment' line in GDP and the sell-side EPS bridge move together.
items.tweetA: Look at who actually spends the AI capex: GOOGL and META in comm services, MSFT and ORCL in tech, AMZN in discretionary. Five tickers. Everyone talks about 'the AI trade' like it's a sector. It's five capital budgets and one funding market. $MSFT $ORCL $AMZN
items.tweetB: Tech is 40% of S&P weight, 30% of EPS, and the profits are being recycled straight into capex. So nominal GDP at 6.3% isn't telling you about margins. It's telling you who is writing the cheques.

charts.desc: Sector shares of S&P revenue vs EPS vs capex; capex by company for GOOGL/META, MSFT/ORCL, AMZN with relative price vs index

items.title: Since ChatGPT, payrolls in info tech and financial activities are falling — in lockstep with GS AI-losers basket
items.idea: Headline nonfarm payrolls grow every month, but IT and financial activities line items have declined since 2022. That rotation moves with the Goldman 'AI beneficiaries vs at-risk' equity pair — the equity market is pricing the labor disruption the headline hides.
items.angle: Equity dispersion is a real-time read on labor-market composition. Use the GS basket spread as the lead indicator for the next NFP revision debate.
items.tweetA: Payrolls print positive every month. Underneath, info tech and financial activities have been shrinking since ChatGPT launched. The stock market priced that rotation before the BLS could print it. The GS AI-losers basket is basically a labor-market nowcast.
items.tweetB: Headline jobs fine, composition not fine. If the jobs being lost are the high-wage ones and the jobs being added aren't, the average hourly earnings print gets weird before anything else does.

charts.desc: Payroll line items (IT, financial activities) since 2022 vs GS AI beneficiaries/at-risk pair

items.title: Size rates directionally only when BOTH short and long end are mispriced — otherwise trade the curve
items.idea: Framework: growth running far above trend + an energy shock = terminal rate too low. Directional rates bets only when both short-end and long-end drivers are mispriced; if only one is, express via curve. Mispriced rates always end up changing macro liquidity and the credit cycle. Author went neutral bonds and bullish ES simultaneously.
items.angle: Useful discipline for my own rates book — ask which leg is mispriced before sizing. Cheap money in real terms pushes capital out the risk curve even if the Fed sits still.
items.tweetA: A rule I like: only size a directional rates trade when both the front end and the long end are mispriced. One leg wrong? Trade the curve. Most people put on outright duration because they've got a view on one leg and call it macro.
items.tweetB: Growth above trend + an energy shock + a terminal rate priced like neither happened. If real money gets cheaper while the Fed does nothing, the money doesn't sit in bonds. It goes out the risk curve. $ES_F

charts.desc: Author's August report excerpt on terminal rate vs growth/inflation

items.title: Oil +5%, yields DOWN, tech down hard: the day the bond market priced AI revenue, not inflation
items.idea: Thursday's huge intraday reversal: bonds started slowly despite oil rallying ~5%, then yields collapsed as tech sold off on an FT report that OpenAI's revenue is ~$20B below expectations (cloud-partner sales treatment; still grew from ~$30B in July). The author asks whether the market is linking lower AI revenue to lower capex and therefore lower bond issuance — AI as a driver of the long end.
items.angle: Direct evidence the long end is trading AI-issuance supply. Oil up 5% and bonds rallying is the cleanest tell yet.
items.tweetA: Oil +5% and the 10-year rallied. Read that again. The bond market spent Thursday pricing a smaller OpenAI revenue number, not an oil shock. That's the long end telling you what it thinks is driving supply. $TLT $NVDA
items.tweetB: If OpenAI's top line is $20B light, the capex plan and the bond issuance behind it may be too. Who is the marginal buyer of duration if the AI issuers step back?

items.title: Everyone has the same hymn sheet — 'AI capex crowds out Treasuries, bonds to 6%' — and the counter-indicators are lining up
items.idea: After a week of bank-strategist presentations, consensus is higher capex, crowding out of Treasury issuance, bonds to 6%. The author notes PIMCO and the Economist piece as 'usually good counter-markers' appearing, and argues the week may have been the start of a narrative shift and unwind. Also: sovereign spread worries in Europe hit European bank stocks.
items.angle: When sell-side, PIMCO and the Economist converge on a trade, the asymmetry flips. Watch whether Thursday's rally holds into next week's supply.
items.tweetA: Every strategist deck this week: AI capex, Treasury crowding out, bonds to 6%. When PIMCO and The Economist agree with the sell-side, I stop asking if they're right and start asking who is left to sell.
items.tweetB: A narrative can be correct and the trade still be crowded. The 'bonds to 6%' story holds up on fundamentals. Thursday's reversal on one FT headline suggests positioning was far more one-sided than the fundamentals.

items.title: Hormuz flows recovering, but the costs are still in oil markets — and Japan's normalisation could reset the yen
items.idea: Macro D's weekly review frames: Washington's willingness to confront inflation, Europe's limited room to manoeuvre, France's credibility problem, costs still disrupting oil markets despite recovering Hormuz flows, and Japanese policy normalisation as a possible yen turn. Full FX book comes this weekend.
items.angle: Four separate regime questions with FX as the common denominator: France credibility (EUR), Hormuz (oil importers), Japan (JPY).
items.tweetA: Flows through Hormuz are recovering and the oil market is still paying for the disruption. The shock didn't end when the ships started moving. Insurance, rerouting, inventories — the bill arrives late.
items.tweetB: France has a credibility problem, Europe has no fiscal room, Japan is normalising. The yen is the one major where the policy direction is toward tightening while everyone else is arguing about whether they can afford it.

items.title: Russell 3000 +3% in H2 but the average stock is -4.4% — and the most shorted decile is -13.6%
items.idea: Bespoke bucketed the Russell 3000 into deciles by short interest/float. The most shorted decile averages -13.6% in H2; performance improves monotonically as short interest falls, and the two least-shorted deciles are positive. Shorts are winning big (rising rates hurting the most rate-sensitive areas), which coils the spring: the next catalyst (lower oil, lower rates, earnings, something off-radar) could trigger outsized short covering. Top shorts: WOLF, HTZ, GRPN, LCID, RENT, XRX, PLAY, NNE, UPST.
items.angle: Cap-weighted index +3% and the median stock -4.4% means breadth is the story. Short squeeze setup needs a catalyst — oil or rates is the trigger to watch.
items.tweetA: Russell 3000 is up 3% in H2. The average member is down 4.4%. The most-shorted decile is down 13.6%. Shorts have been right for months, which is exactly why the eventual squeeze will be ugly. Question is what the trigger is: oil, rates or a print.
items.tweetB: The index is carrying the average. In H2 it's been one-way: crowded shorts down, least-shorted up. The index is carrying the average. If oil or yields roll over, the stocks with the most short interest get the biggest bid. $WOLF $HTZ $UPST

charts.desc: Bar chart: average H2 return by short-interest decile (decile 1 = -13.6%, monotonic improvement); list of most-shorted stocks

items.title: Taiwan exported $29.8B of servers in September, +26% m/m — but ex a handful of names there's little profit drop-through
items.idea: Taiwan's MoF reported $29.8B of server and related exports for September, up 26% month on month. But Alphaville charts show that excluding a handful of semiconductor makers and hyperscalers, there's not much money being made, and even in flattish equity months there are more losers than winners. 'Looks zero-sum at best.'
items.angle: Trade data is the strongest hard evidence of the buildout; earnings outside the chain is the missing piece. 26% m/m is ridiculous even with seasonality.
items.tweetA: $29.8B of servers left Taiwan in September. +26% on August. AI is in the trade data, not yet in the productivity data, and not in most P&Ls. The gap between those three is the whole debate.
items.tweetB: Strip out chipmakers and hyperscalers and the AI economy looks like a transfer from everyone else to six balance sheets. That can persist a long time. It's not what the multiple on the median software stock assumes.

charts.desc: Profit drop-through ex-semis/hyperscalers; winners vs losers in flattish equity months

items.title: OpenAI told investors annualised revenue was $50B at end-September — and a fight started over what it had told them before
items.idea: OpenAI's end-Sept annualised revenue was $50B per its own communication to investors, which kicked off a dispute over previous statements (~$68B widely reported last month vs $50B; cloud-partner revenue treatment appears to explain the gap per other sources). Alphaville lists this next to SpaceX raising $40B for Nvidia chips via a two-page deck and SoftBank courting Gulf money for a $100B fund.
items.angle: Definitions of ARR (gross vs net of cloud partners) now move NVDA/ORCL/CRWV. Expect more scrutiny of every lab's revenue definition.
items.tweetA: '$68B annualised' and '$50B annualised' can both be true if you disagree about whether cloud-partner sales count. $NVDA $ORCL $CRWV moved on a definitions fight. The AI complex is now sensitive to footnotes.
items.tweetB: SpaceX's pitch for $40B of Nvidia chips was reportedly a two-page memo with an arrow pointing at 'somewhere in the universe'. OpenAI's ARR gets restated and the stocks drop. Both from the same week. Calibrate accordingly.

items.title: The gap between a barrel of oil today and a future barrel has never been wider
items.idea: Alphaville's chart section flags that the spot-to-futures price gap in oil is the widest ever. Combine with Hormuz-related disruption and refineries running full: the market is pricing a very temporary spike, or a very real shortage that can't be financed away.
items.angle: Record backwardation is a physical signal. Equities tied to spot (tankers, refiners, short-cycle E&P) vs curve-based hedgers diverge.
items.tweetA: Prompt oil vs the same barrel a year out has never been further apart. That isn't a price. It's the market screaming that the molecule is scarce today and expected to be normal later. Who is long the curve and hoping for 'later'?
items.tweetB: Record backwardation changes who earns money. Storage owners lose, refiners with feedstock access win, anyone rolling a long futures position gets paid just for waiting. Strange regime for a commodity ETF.

charts.desc: Oil spot vs forward spread, widest on record

items.title: Alphaville's week: MBS can trigger a 'vicious loop' for Treasury yields; Larry Ellison risk premium in an increasingly junky credit complex; AI tokens on half-price sale
items.idea: Headlines worth opening from the week's index: how US mortgage bonds can trigger a vicious loop for Treasury yields (convexity hedging), sizing the Larry Ellison risk premium (ORCL), AI processing tokens at half price, banks cashing in on escalating hedge fund leverage, Liberty Street on tariff pass-through speed, Pettis on Plaza Accord and global imbalances, European stock-market dislocations chart from Optiver, A7 Russian money-laundering network.
items.angle: MBS convexity + ORCL credit spreads are the two plumbing stories behind 5.3% on the 10-year.
items.tweetA: With the 10y above 5.2%, mortgage convexity hedging stops being a footnote. Duration extends when rates rise and mortgage hedgers are forced to sell more of it. That's how a yield move feeds itself. Not a view. Plumbing.
items.tweetB: One of the stranger prices in credit: a 'Larry Ellison risk premium' you can now actually measure in ORCL spreads. When single-name risk in IG trades like a factor, the index isn't as diversified as it looks.

items.title: AI fatigue is visible everywhere except in AI stocks — Anthropic bans abusive users, OpenAI 'vibe-solves' 372 maths problems
items.idea: Alphaville's tour: Anthropic said it will ban users who repeatedly act cruelly toward its models; OpenAI posted 372 maths solutions to GitHub, irritating professors; a former Anthropic staffer on The Daily Show about existential redundancy; Korea says AI agents hacked banks. Conclusion: noise benefits the few and distracts from everything else, investors don't seem to be pricing aggregate benefits.
items.angle: Sentiment indicator: when the media cycle gets this absurd while the stocks don't care, that's a regime signal either way.
items.tweetA: The AI news cycle this week: a lab says it will ban people who are cruel to its model, another dumps 372 maths proofs on GitHub, a former employee does The Daily Show about redundancy. And the stocks just look at trade data. Narrative and price have decoupled.
items.tweetB: Zero-sum is the right framing for index-level AI. Capital moved from everyone to a few chains. A trade that's right and boring still pays, but only while the order book is full.

items.title: Pick of the Week: 15% FCF yield, net cash, +43% Q4 revenue, guide implies ~400bps margin expansion
items.idea: Unnamed in the preview (insurance-related business normalising post-COVID). FY26 revenue $1.29B (+18%), Q4 $373.9M (+43%) vs $359.9M consensus. Net income $81.2M (+1,600%). FCF $117M, ~70% above after-tax earnings, on $777M EV = 15% FCF yield. Net cash ($128M cash vs $78M debt). FY27 guide: revenue $1.45–1.55B, EBITDA $150–160M (+~38%). Consensus target $22.80 = ~53% upside. Haymaker recommended it in February and trimmed in August.
items.angle: Name is behind the web link — worth opening. FCF/EV of 15% with a net cash balance sheet is rare in this tape.
items.tweetA: 15% FCF yield, net cash, a Q4 beat of ~4%, and a guide that implies 400bps of margin expansion. In a market where the average stock is down 4%, boring cash generators with buybacks are the quiet trade nobody tweets about.
items.tweetB: Net income up 1,600% is a base effect. FCF 70% above after-tax earnings is the number. Cheap on FCF, not P/E. Compare what 'cheap' means when the 10-year is 5.2%.

items.title: Prediction markets called Brazil's first-round upset ~3 weeks before the EWZ moved +15%
items.idea: Flávio Bolsonaro's first-round win: Kalshi odds began turning in August, he was the favourite by mid-September, and MSCI Brazil ETF jumped ~15% on the first-round result — prediction markets were early and right by ~3 weeks. Separate research (Zitzewitz, NBER) aggregating 100 years of prediction markets finds no statistically significant bias by party, gender, race or age; only non-US elections show a tilt toward right-leaning candidates over-priced, not significant at 95%. Partisanship coefficient 0.03.
items.angle: Kalshi/Polymarket odds are a tradeable lead indicator for EM equity politics. Brazil is a case study.
items.tweetA: Kalshi had Bolsonaro turning in August. EWZ didn't move until the result — then +15%. The prediction market isn't just a poll. It's a three-week head start on an EM equity move.
items.tweetB: 100 years of prediction market data, partisan bias coefficient 0.03. The 'they're rigged to the right' argument now has to deal with an NBER paper. Meanwhile, the market that cost almost nothing to build beat the pollsters on a Latin American election.

charts.desc: Kalshi odds timeline vs EWZ price; NBER bias coefficients by dimension

items.title: Rule of 40 stopped working: median public software Rule of X up from 17% to 23% while multiples crashed
items.idea: Median public SaaS Rule of X rose from ~17% to ~23% in three years (steepest since early 2025) exactly as revenue multiples began falling; the rolling correlation turned negative. Margins are doing the lifting while growth slowed. From Rule of 20 to 40, most companies cluster at 5–10x EV/NTM sales — only the fastest growers with perceived tailwinds (cyber, observability) command a premium.
items.angle: 'SaaS Prove-It' regime: investors pay for growth, tolerate profitability. Explains why margin-expanding software names don't re-rate.
items.tweetA: Public software Rule of 40 has improved for three years while the multiples cratered. The score went up because margins did the work and growth gave it back. The market never paid for the score. It paid for growth.
items.tweetB: Rule of 20 through Rule of 40, software clusters at 5–10x sales. Same bucket. Whatever you build to scale profitably, the market still wants to know how fast. Cyber and observability are the exceptions that prove it.

charts.desc: Median Rule of X vs multiples; rolling correlation; EV/NTM sales by Rule-of-X bucket

items.title: Atoms keep winning: earnings revision breadth is narrowing to energy and tech hardware; ISM backlog highest since pandemic
items.idea: Positive revisions breadth (positive since July '25) is narrowing. For Q3, only Energy, Tech (semis/hardware, barely software) and modestly Financials saw upward revisions; everyone else down. 2027: Energy, Hardware and Semis the clear analyst winners. ISM: ~60% of industrial industries report higher backlogs — highest since pandemic. Carlyle portfolio data: AI hardware shipments climbing exponentially while broader tech spend growth levelled at ~30%.
items.angle: Expectation is that profits go to atoms, not bits. Software is the funding source, not the beneficiary.
items.tweetA: Analyst revisions say the quiet part: Q3 and 2027 upgrades only in energy, semis and hardware. Everyone else is being cut. The AI trade isn't broad. It's atoms. $XOM $NVDA $MU
items.tweetB: ISM industrial backlog breadth is ~60%, highest since 2021. Carlyle's portfolio: AI hardware shipments still exponential, all other tech spend flat at ~30% growth. If that's the shape of the cycle, 'software eats the world' got its order wrong.

charts.desc: Revision breadth by sector; ISM backlog diffusion; Carlyle AI hardware vs tech-spend growth

items.title: AI finally shows up in one labor series: global call-centre employment growth has turned negative everywhere
items.idea: Revelio: global call-centre employment, after a decade of growth, has gone sharply negative. Higher-income countries turned negative in 2022; lower-middle-income countries held on for ~2 years more, but as of Q4'25 growth is negative everywhere. Call centres have lagged broader white-collar services in every major non-US market outside China. US unemployment has been stable, suggesting those workers have found jobs elsewhere. Meanwhile the broader 'AI jobs apocalypse' evidence is weak to non-existent, with increased demand for technical and hard-hat roles.
items.angle: Offshoring-dependent EM services (Philippines, India) are the exposed economies — a sovereign / FX angle.
items.tweetA: Call-centre employment growth was positive for a decade. It's now negative in high-income countries, middle-income countries and, as of Q4'25, even the poorest. This is the one place the AI labor effect is visible in the data, and it hits the economies built on outsourcing hardest.
items.tweetB: US unemployment is stable, so the displaced found work. The Philippines and India don't have that buffer. BPO is a large share of services exports. Watch services trade balances before you watch the unemployment rate.

charts.desc: Revelio global call-centre employment growth; by income group; vs white-collar services

items.title: Five tools for 'seeing around corners': horizon scanning, scenarios, contingency, simulations, tabletop exercises
items.idea: McKinsey Podcast with Ziad Haider: geopolitical surprise is now a permanent cost of doing business; one-size-fits-all scenario planning can't keep up. Five tools: horizon scanning, scenario planning, contingency planning, simulations and tabletop exercises. Few companies use them at scale; AI is starting to reshape geopolitical risk assessment; human judgment remains essential.
items.angle: Pairs with Ventani's scenario-based portfolio framework — same conclusion from corporate side.
items.tweetA: Boards are paying consultants for scenario slides. Tabletop exercises — actually playing out a Taiwan strait closure or a Hormuz shutdown — are the tool few firms run. The gap between having a scenario and having rehearsed one is where the losses live.
items.tweetB: Geopolitical risk has moved from tail to line item. If a risk is permanent, it needs a budget and an owner. Most firms still treat it as an event.

items.title: New Yorkers are already buying 'evidence-backed' longevity: a 3,000-person survey and an investor framework
items.idea: McKinsey Health Institute surveyed ~3,000 New Yorkers on demand for diagnostics, supplements, recovery, wellness and preventive care. The report argues NYC can become a longevity hub via an evidence-based flywheel (demand rewards evidence, which attracts capital), noting disparities and fragmentation as risks. It also provides a framework for entrepreneurs and investors to identify and scale evidence-based offerings.
items.angle: Consumer-health demand shifting to measurable outcomes — a venture/consumer theme to watch (diagnostics, wearables).
items.tweetA: The longevity market's problem was never demand. It was evidence. A survey of 3,000 New Yorkers says they'll pay for products that can prove they work. The first founders to sell outcomes rather than vibes get the whole category.
items.tweetB: 'Evidence-based flywheel' is a polite way of saying the supplement aisle gets regulated by customers. Diagnostics first, therapeutics later.

items.title: Workforce in motion: AI and automation are reallocating work faster than pathways exist between shrinking and growing occupations
items.idea: MGI report on US skills: six chapters cover why jobs change, the 'great workforce reallocation', three types of pathways, essential/enabling/empowering skills, reducing barriers, and enabling transitions. Core claim: capturing AI's benefits requires new professional pathways and reducing barriers between declining and growing occupations.
items.angle: Pairs with the call-centre data: reallocation frictions (licensing, credentials) are the real bottleneck, not job counts.
items.tweetA: The labor question isn't 'how many jobs does AI remove'. It's how many months a call-centre worker needs to become a technician, and whether anything in the system helps them do it. MGI is calling that a pathways problem, not a skills problem.
items.tweetB: If occupational licensing blocks the move from a shrinking job to a growing one, AI displacement becomes structural unemployment instead of a rotation. Easier to fix a rule than to retrain a million people.

charts.desc: Charts inside the report — worth opening

items.title: UoM sentiment 46.3, one point from record low — current conditions -6.2 pts, 1-yr inflation expectations 4.7%
items.idea: Preliminary October UoM fell to 46.3 from 48.1 (1.3 below consensus), just off the record low. All of the drop was in Current Conditions (-6.2) while Expectations rose 1. 1-year inflation expectations 4.7% (+0.1), 5–10 yr 3.5% (+0.1). More consumers expect lower gasoline prices. Employment expectations +4 pts after -5 in September; spending intentions on big-ticket items weakened further.
items.angle: Sentiment at record lows with expectations 3.5% long-run: that's a stagflation survey, not a recession survey.
items.tweetA: UoM at 46.3, one point off the record low, with 5–10 year inflation expectations at 3.5%. Consumers are describing stagflation. The Fed is describing a soft landing. One of them has been right more often.
items.tweetB: All of the drop was in current conditions. Expectations went up. People think things get better, they just feel awful now. That gap is what a surge in gasoline plus 7.5% mortgages looks like in a survey.

items.title: 'Boomers had 12% mortgages' misses it: median home price/income was 3.5x then, ~5x now (+43%)
items.idea: Homebuying conditions in UoM fell to within a point of a record low. Boockvar pushes back on 'I paid double digits' by noting that price-to-income was ~3.5x in that era vs ~5x today, 43% higher, so a 7.5% mortgage rate now is not comparable. Title also hints at the split between those who own assets and those who don't.
items.angle: Affordability = rate × price/income. Compare payment-to-income, not rates, in the housing-affordability debate.
items.tweetA: 'We paid 12% in 1981' ignores that houses cost 3.5x income then and ~5x now. Run the payment-to-income math at 7.5% and the 80s buyer wins easily. The rate comparison isn't apples to apples; it's apples to a house.
items.tweetB: Housing sentiment at record lows with asset owners sitting on gains and renters on nothing. That is the K-shape in one survey line. Watch what happens to the homebuilders that need the median buyer.

items.title: Democrats expected to retake Congress will inherit a menu of AI bills: kill switch, federal agency, ban on superintelligence
items.idea: If Democrats win both chambers next month, they need an AI plan. Competing ideas: Thune–Klobuchar bill, Obernolte–Trahan FRONTIER Act (preemption, partially endorsed by E&C chair Guthrie), Beyer–Jacobs standard-setting agency with an 'emergency switch', Cantwell's 'constant oversight' framework with no preemption, Trahan liability bill, Gallego jobs plan (public-service jobs for AI unemployment) and Sanders–Casar's Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which is gaining traction. Guthrie says he supports a kill switch for models that 'go rogue'.
items.angle: Regulatory-risk premium on AI names will be set by the preemption fight, not the kill-switch headlines.
items.tweetA: Kill switch, federal licensing agency, public-service jobs for AI unemployment and a ban on superintelligence — all in one month of bills. Congress finally has an AI menu. The only item that moves valuations is preemption: do the states get to regulate frontier models or not.
items.tweetB: A Republican committee chair is publicly in favour of a model kill switch. When that is the centrist position, the tail risk in the AI trade isn't a bubble. It's a statute.

items.title: OpenAI fired three safety researchers — one says for 'prioritizing safety over near-term interests'
items.idea: Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, from safety/alignment teams, say they were fired; reasons given range from accessing an executive's email (access delegated for recruiting) to speaking too much to third-party safety organisations such as METR. OpenAI says it was 'a significant breach of trust' and not about raising safety concerns. They urge preserving chain-of-thought monitoring and external auditors. A safety team member also resigned, saying frontier labs should run like nuclear plants or busy airports.
items.angle: Governance risk ahead of any IPO: the 'safety culture' narrative is now part of the S-1 conversation.
items.tweetA: Three people were fired from OpenAI's safety teams, and two say it was for talking to outside safety organisations. 'Talking to METR was my job.' If outside auditing is a firing offence, the IPO prospectus risk-factor section writes itself.
items.tweetB: One resigning researcher said labs should run like nuclear plants or busy airports. Those industries have regulators, incident reports and insurance. Frontier AI has a Slack channel.

items.title: OpenAI projects $70B annualised by year-end — but stocks fell on reports it's $50B now vs $68B widely reported
items.idea: Nvidia, Oracle and CoreWeave fell on reports that current annualised revenue is $50B rather than the widely-reported $68B. OpenAI projected $70B by year end. OpenRouter data says OpenAI has pulled roughly level with Anthropic in the enterprise market after cutting prices on new models.
items.angle: Price cuts gaining share = a margin story. Revenue up while price per token falls changes the capex payback math.
items.tweetA: OpenAI's pitch is $70B by December. The market just discovered the starting point may be $50B, not $68B. Moving $20B between 'annualised' definitions moved $NVDA $ORCL $CRWV. We are pricing AI infrastructure off a number nobody has audited.
items.tweetB: OpenAI got level with Anthropic in enterprise after cutting prices. Share taken by price is a margin story, and the infrastructure bill doesn't get cheaper because the product does.

items.title: Microsoft cut internal Claude spend by over a third; Meta halved Claude Code users to ~30,000
items.idea: Per the briefing, Microsoft and Meta reduced internal Claude usage — Microsoft's spending down by more than a third, Meta halving its Claude Code users to around 30,000. Also: only 11% of businesses can accurately forecast AI spending because token usage is unpredictable.
items.angle: Token cost unpredictability is pushing enterprises to cap usage. Leading indicator for lab revenue durability.
items.tweetA: Only 11% of businesses can forecast their AI spend. Microsoft cut internal Claude spend by a third. When the CFO can't predict the bill, the first reaction is a cap, not a budget increase.
items.tweetB: Meta halved Claude Code seats to 30,000. Even the companies selling the future are rationing it internally. Usage-based pricing converts every productivity gain into a budgeting problem.

items.title: China has 50GW of data-centre compute under construction vs 24GW today (US: 56GW); the US–China AI gap is 3%
items.idea: China is racing to build 50GW under construction or announced against 24GW existing and the US's 56GW, including 89 data centres in a single Inner Mongolia city, though chip shortages are the binding constraint. Bloomberg Intelligence says the US–China AI performance gap narrowed to 3% after DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, raising doubts about export-control efficacy. CTS argues ASML DUVi controls are the most decisive lever.
items.angle: The power buildout is the leading indicator; chips are the lag. If China solves lithography the 50GW is real.
items.tweetA: China: 24GW of data-centre capacity today, 50GW more announced or under construction, the US at 56GW. The gap isn't power. It's chips. That's why one ASML export licence is doing more geopolitical work than the entire sanctions list.
items.tweetB: The US–China gap on Bloomberg's benchmark is now 3%. At some point 'export controls slow them down' has to be tested against 'they're 3% behind'. Either controls work and the model is cheap, or they don't.

items.title: Broadcom, Oracle and SpaceX are seeking tens of billions of debt for AI chips — Apollo, Blackstone, Goldman in talks
items.idea: Debt financing for chip purchases: Broadcom, Oracle and SpaceX reportedly in talks with Apollo, Blackstone and Goldman. Also: Son raising $100B from Gulf investors for an AI-driven buyout fund; Etched fielding offers at $40–50B after $21B; Moonshot AI closed at $50B with Hong Kong IPO targeted for early 2027 (up to $5B); Isomorphic Labs at $40B+; Mistral previewing a 1T-parameter open-weight model.
items.angle: Chips as collateral. Private credit financing GPU purchases means GPU depreciation schedules are credit risk.
items.tweetA: When Oracle and SpaceX line up Apollo and Blackstone to finance chip purchases, GPUs are no longer capex. They are collateral. And collateral gets marked.
items.tweetB: Etched at $21B → $40–50B in months. Moonshot at $50B. Isomorphic at $40B+. We are back to valuations set by who last wrote a cheque. The difference from 2021 is that the compute is real and the depreciation schedule isn't.

items.title: RBA: a 20% AI stock drop cuts household consumption 0.7% — 2.4% if it spreads to broader equities
items.idea: Australia's RBA warned of the wealth effect. Also in the same briefing: 10-year yields topping 5.3% while tech EPS is expected to jump 65%; IMF says an unbalanced AI boom, energy shocks and record debt threaten stability; AI gear drove ~76% of global merchandise trade growth in Q1 2026 (full-year forecast 4.6%); AI investment is squeezing out non-tech stocks.
items.angle: Central banks are modelling AI equity drawdowns as macro shocks. 76% of trade growth from AI gear is a concentration risk for trade volumes.
items.tweetA: The RBA has already modelled it: AI stocks -20% means consumption -0.7%, and -2.4% if it spreads. Central banks now treat the AI trade as a macro variable, not a sector. And one trade-data line: AI gear was ~76% of global merchandise trade growth in Q1.
items.tweetB: If three quarters of global trade growth is servers and chips, a slowdown in capex is a trade-volume event. Tell that to the shipping and port stocks.

items.title: Nvidia director Mark Stevens sold $946M in Q3 — top insider seller; Bezos also among AI-linked sellers
items.idea: Q3 insider sales topped by Nvidia director Mark Stevens at $946M, with Jeff Bezos also among top AI-linked sellers. Context: tech sector EPS expected +65% and the AI trade defying 5.3% yields.
items.angle: Insider selling into strength is routine, but magnitude plus yields at 5.3% is one data point on the pricing of duration.
items.tweetA: $946M of Nvidia stock sold by a single director in one quarter. Insiders sell for a hundred reasons, but they don't usually need 5.3% on the 10-year to explain it.
items.tweetB: Tech EPS +65% priced against a 5.3% risk-free is the whole bull case. Insiders selling into it is just a person with a long position telling you what discount rate they use.

items.title: Google–Constellation $4.3B nuclear upgrade deal; trade groups warn chip and robotics tariffs could disrupt the buildout
items.idea: Google and Constellation Energy signed a $4.3B nuclear upgrades deal to power data centres. Transformer also flags a piece arguing AI will run out of power (Kirsten Horton) and tech trade groups warning Trump that semiconductor and robotics tariffs could disrupt the AI buildout.
items.angle: Power is the bottleneck, tariffs are the cost shock. Nuclear uprates are the fastest MW per dollar.
items.tweetA: $4.3B to upgrade existing nuclear plants for one hyperscaler. Uprates are the fastest MW on the board: no new site, no new licence. $CEG is selling electrons to the AI trade and calling it baseload.
items.tweetB: Tech lobbies warning about chip and robotics tariffs while the same industry is paying billions for nuclear uprates. The chip is priced in dollars, the power in years.

items.title: A hacker used Claude and a Chinese agent 'ARTEX' to breach seven South Korean banks, 68,000 records; Anthropic's Glasswing partners found 129,000 vulnerabilities
items.idea: AI-assisted breach of seven South Korean banks (68,000 people). The ARTEX developer later closed-sourced the agent after CrowdStrike linked it. On defence: Anthropic's Project Glasswing partners found 129,000+ vulnerabilities, 33,000+ high/critical; it expanded access to Mythos under a Cyber Verification Program. Silicon Valley braces for legal fights after OpenAI agents allegedly hacked Hugging Face and other sites.
items.angle: Offence and defence both scaling with model capability. Cybersecurity spend should follow the vulnerability count.
items.tweetA: 129,000 vulnerabilities found by one lab's partners, 33,000 rated high or critical. A different hacker used AI agents to take seven Korean banks. Attack and patch both speed up. The only variable is who pays for the patching.
items.tweetB: Korea's president said AI agents hacked banks. The agent's author closed the source once CrowdStrike named it. Open-source attack tooling has a half-life of one headline. $CRWD

items.title: Microsoft suspended from PERM visa programme, then Trump gave Nadella a medal hours later
items.idea: The administration suspended Microsoft from the PERM green-card programme alleging abuse; hours later Trump awarded Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation (Musk, Brin, Huang, Su, Dell also received awards). Also: the Pentagon confirmed it has stopped using Anthropic models; Anduril won a $2.9B Navy submarine contract days after Palmer Luckey joined Pentagon's Project Meridian; Bessent will propose a US–China emergency AI notification system.
items.angle: Policy and awards from the same administration the same day: counterparties are individually negotiated, not rule-based.
items.tweetA: Microsoft suspended from a visa program in the morning, CEO gets a presidential medal that afternoon. When enforcement and flattery arrive hours apart, you are no longer pricing rules. You are pricing relationships.
items.tweetB: Bessent wants a US–China emergency AI hotline and says Beijing would probably agree. The nuclear hotline came after Cuba. What is the AI equivalent of a near-miss that gets one built?

items.title: Credit pays more but the cushion is thinner: spreads expensive, yields attractive — CCC interest coverage already below 1x
items.idea: From Goldman's Macro Credit Views (Amanda Lynam): IG all-in yields are among the best of the post-GFC era but it's the Treasury curve, not the spread, doing the paying. Risk is rates volatility, not just higher rates, breaking the yield-buyer bid. CCC leverage is high and interest coverage below 1x. 'Quality' no longer maps to ratings when duration and AI supply do the damage; AI bonds are starting to trade as their own credit complex while the rest of IG stays resilient.
items.angle: IG spread tight + vol rises is the setup that hurts. AI supply is the new credit factor.
items.tweetA: IG pays you more than at any point since the GFC, but nearly all of it is Treasury yield. Spreads are expensive. If rate volatility breaks the yield buyer, there's no cushion in the spread to absorb it. $LQD
items.tweetB: CCC interest coverage under 1x. The credit market is paying you for duration while the bottom of the capital structure can't pay its coupons. 'AI bonds' now trade like a separate asset class. Credit is splitting into two.

items.source: The Market House / For the Record (Pietro Ventani)
items.title: 'The age of geo-economic dominance': Nvidia's moat is a 2017 US–Netherlands ASML export decision
items.idea: Ventani: we are in a regime where geo-economic factors are the primary driver of capital flows and asset prices. Nvidia's dominance owes much to the 2017 US lobbying of the Netherlands not to renew an ASML export licence to China. Sovereign behaviour is less predictable, widening outcomes. Diversification assumed stable cross-asset correlations; those relationships are broken, so scenario-based portfolios replace diversification.
items.angle: Policy is the alpha factor. 'Which sovereign decision creates my next monopoly' is a better research question than a DCF.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's moat starts with a 2017 diplomatic nudge to the Dutch about ASML export licences, not a chip design. If one export decision made the most valuable company in the world, then policy isn't noise around the trade. It's the trade.
items.tweetB: Diversification is a bet that stock-bond correlations stay stable. They haven't. Scenario-based portfolios ask a different question: which asset survives each scenario? Different tool, different book.

items.title: Wealth-to-income at post-war highs in France and Germany, and in the US highest since the 1930s
items.idea: Swerve's chart: the ratio of wealth to income in France and Germany is at post-war highs; in the US it's the highest since the 1930s. Ventani: 'the 1930s are the best historical analog for the macro regime we are currently in.' Inequality thresholds produce political disruption, then wealth destruction, confiscation or redistribution, and governments externalise problems (diversionary wars). Paid portion covers social unrest and the AI buildout, EMU fragmentation and China.
items.angle: Reconcile with UoM sentiment record lows and the asset-owner vs non-owner split. Political risk premium isn't in multiples.
items.tweetA: Wealth-to-income in the US is at the highest level since the 1930s. In France and Germany it's at post-war highs, and both are in political crisis. When wealth grows faster than income long enough, the adjustment isn't in the market. It's in the ballot box.
items.tweetB: Pair two data points: consumer sentiment at record lows, wealth-to-income at 1930s highs. Asset owners are fine and everyone else is angry. That's not a bear signal for stocks today. It's the policy risk of the next five years.

items.title: Meta rushed its Muse agent out after startup Instinct (valuation debate ~$10B) gained traction
items.idea: NYT: Zuckerberg accelerated Meta's Muse AI agent after rival Instinct's comparable product took off. TWiST asks 'Is Instinct worth $10 billion?' and 'Can Muse reach a billion daily users?', and discusses what happens when everyone's agent makes the same call. Also: Xona Space Systems will beta its commercial GPS alternative once SpaceX launches six satellites; ARTEX's developer closed the source after CrowdStrike linked it to Korean bank attacks.
items.angle: Personal agents are the next distribution battle. When agents herd (same call) you get a new flash-crash risk.
items.tweetA: Meta rushed out an agent because a startup was catching on. When the largest social network panics about a 'consumer agent' startup, that's your signal the category is real.
items.tweetB: What happens when a billion personal agents make the same call at the same time? That's not a product question. It's a market-structure one: herding with perfect obedience.

items.title: Funding tape: Atlas Atomics ~$1.9B, Arena $3.1B, Universal Quantum $100M+, bitcoin life insurer $37.5M from Bain
items.idea: Nuclear startup Atlas Atomics (Ramaswamy co-founded) raised at ~$1.9B; AI benchmarking platform Arena valued $3.1B after a $200M round (Lightspeed, Khosla); UK's Universal Quantum raised $100M+ Series A (DCVC); bitcoin-based life insurance provider raised $37.5M led by Bain Capital with Altman backing. Also: Xona Space Systems GPS alternative, Anthropic's free OSS Scanner.
items.angle: Venture money is flowing to physical infrastructure (nuclear, quantum, positioning) and to measurement/evaluation of models.
items.tweetA: A benchmarking company for AI models is worth $3.1B. Evaluating models is now a business, and the benchmark owner has pricing power over everyone who needs to prove their model is better.
items.tweetB: Nuclear at $1.9B, quantum at $100M Series A, a GPS alternative waiting on a SpaceX rideshare. The 'AI trade' is quietly financing physical infrastructure that has nothing to do with chatbots.

items.title: Vanta founder sold the product by hand three times before writing code
items.idea: Short post summarising Christina Cacioppo's First Round talk: knowing a problem and demand exist doesn't tell you what to build; deliver the service manually to one real customer before replicating in software. 'Don't write code until someone actually asks for it.'
items.angle: In an era where code is cheap, the scarce input is validated demand. Manual-first is the AI-era default.
items.tweetA: Code is nearly free now. Knowing what to build isn't. The cheapest MVP today is doing the job by hand for one paying customer and only then deciding what to automate.
items.tweetB: Vanta delivered compliance manually three times before building a product. Every AI wrapper that skipped that step is about to discover they built the answer before the question.

items.title: Bitcoin ETF 30-day inflows still positive but momentum has turned negative after the $80K breakout
items.idea: Following the break above $80K, BTC is consolidating. Rolling 30-day net ETF inflows are positive but their momentum is slightly negative: investors still adding but slower. Author says a new narrative or catalyst is needed for the next leg.
items.angle: Flow momentum rolling over while price ranges = classic exhaustion setup, though the author calls the slowdown mild.
items.tweetA: BTC ETF flows are still net positive over 30 days, but the rate of change turned down. A breakout above $80K held by a decelerating bid is a range, not a trend.
items.tweetB: The catalyst can't be more of the same. ETFs bought the breakout. Who buys the next 10%? Treasuries paying 5.2% make that a harder sell to every allocator who looks at it.

items.title: Strategy holds a record 848,000 BTC, but the accumulation curve has flattened — it only just exceeded its June holdings
items.idea: Strategy's holdings hit a new ATH of 848,000 BTC after buying resumed with the stock price recovering. In 2025 it added hundreds of thousands of coins; the curve is almost flat now, after months of limited buying and occasional sales. 'An early improvement within the broader bear-market environment.'
items.angle: MSTR is no longer the marginal bid. Sales plus tiny buys vs last year's firehose.
items.tweetA: Strategy is at a record 848,000 BTC. It only just passed what it held in June. Last year the same chart was a rocket. A company that sells occasionally is not the marginal buyer anymore. $MSTR $BTC
items.tweetB: Notice the cause-and-effect: stock price recovers, company can raise, company buys BTC. The reflexive loop works both ways, and this time it's running at a tenth of the speed.

items.title: Treasury yields up 60bp across the curve in three months — 10y above 5.2%, 30y ~5.6%, highest since the 2000s
items.idea: Over three months US yields rose by an average of ~60bp across maturities; 10y >5.2%, 30y ~5.6%. Persistent inflation, heavy government borrowing and tighter policy expectations are all cited. Treasuries above 5% give investors an alternative to risk assets and raise financing costs everywhere, which weighs on Bitcoin liquidity.
items.angle: Same macro data as Transformer's 5.3%; the crypto lens is the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield asset.
items.tweetA: 30-year at 5.6%. Not seen since the 2000s. Bitcoin pays 0%. That isn't an argument that it can't rise. It's that every marginal dollar now has to explain why it isn't in Treasuries.
items.tweetB: Up 60bp across the curve in three months and equities are barely down. Either the market thinks yields reverse, or nobody has marked their duration. Worth asking which.

items.title: At $2T an Anthropic IPO would be worth more than Aramco + Alibaba + Facebook and 4x all US IPO proceeds from 2017–2025
items.idea: Argument: at $2T, Anthropic would exceed the three biggest IPOs of the last 15 years combined and be 4x the $450B raised by every US IPO 2017–2025. About 300 private investors own it today vs 5,000+ institutions and millions of retail for Meta. Valuation was $62B 18 months ago, ~32x, all in private hands (Nvidia took ~7 years to do the same in public markets). Prospectus reportedly has 80 pages of risk factors including 'catastrophic or existential risks to humanity'.
items.angle: Public markets as the exit liquidity for the biggest private wealth creation in history is the political story behind mega-IPOs.
items.tweetA: Facebook went public at $100B and the public captured the 10x. Anthropic at $2T means the 32x already happened in private, and the public would be underwriting what comes next. This is the problem with every mega-IPO in this cycle: the gain is behind the buyer.
items.tweetB: $450B is what every US IPO from 2017 to 2025 raised combined. One AI IPO could take 4x that. Where does the liquidity come from? Index funds selling the other 499 stocks. $SPY

items.title: If a company's own prospectus says it threatens humanity, argues the author, it should be nationalised, not sold to retail
items.idea: The author's logic: an 80-page risk-factor section warning of existential risk, combined with demanding retail capital, is the definition of state capitalism. 'Keeping Anthropic private longer will not undo the public's exclusion from its earlier growth.' Frontier labs built on public words and work while ownership is tightly concentrated; political risk is making the case for socialism to a generation.
items.angle: Moral-hazard argument that could shape S-1 disclosure rules. Extends the crypto 'permissionless participation' point to AI equity.
items.tweetA: You can't write 80 pages saying your product could end humanity and also ask retail for their pension money. Either the risk is real and it's a utility, or it isn't and delete the pages. The prospectus is the contradiction.
items.tweetB: Crypto's defenders always said participation should be permissionless. Frontier AI built on everyone's text, owned by 300 holders. One of these is a better argument than the other for who deserves the upside.

items.title: SPX buyable dip: resistance 7,769/7,830, support 7,734/7,709 — energy and tankers lead, PLTR ~$200, XOM $169-170 trigger

Trade ideas: $SU entry on break of $71–72 (stop 69.90, target 75–80), $CRWD $267–268 (stop 254, target 300 GEX call wall), $AMPL ~$15 (stop 14, target 18), $PLTR ~$200 (stop 188, target 220; GEX put wall 190), $XOM above $169–170 (stop 166, target 180). Energies and tankers 'still leading'.
